5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20), the disease caused by germline *TNFAIP3* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *TNFAIP3* variant or an HA20 (A20 haploinsufficiency) diagnosis;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *TNFAIP3* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". Quote that statement in `parental_testing_statement`. Use `inherited unspecified parent` when it says a parent carries it without saying which.
149	- **Otherwise:** `not reported`. Do not infer from a pedigree drawing or from an affected but untested parent.
150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.
151	
152	### When the paper describes no in-scope person
153	For example, a review without patient-level detail, or a paper about something else:
154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;
156	- leave the other tables empty.
157	
158	### Large papers
159	If the output is long, you may build it in parts with a short Python script and combine the parts.
160	- Every value must still come from your reading of the paper.
161	- If a script transcribes a table, check its output against the table and say so in `method_note`.
162	- Use only your own scratch directory (given in your task) for temporary files.
163

165	1. Validate that your file parses as JSON.
166	2. Check every span occurs verbatim in the paper.
167	3. Check every row has every schema field.
168	4. Reply with:
169	   - the number of rows per table;
170	   - the number of individuals;
171	   - anything you were unsure how to record.

8	# T-cell and monocyte DNA methylation and Wnt dysregulation in common variable immunodeficiency: an exploratory study
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	BackgroundMany patients with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) develop inflammatory/autoimmune complications associated with T-cell and monocyte dysregulation which may involve epigenetic modifications.ObjectiveTo characterize genome-wide CpG methylation in CD3^+ T-cells and CD14^+ monocytes in CVID and relate epigenetic alterations to gene expression and circulating proteins.MethodsWhole-genome bisulphite sequencing was performed on purified CD3^+ T-cells and CD14^+ monocytes from three CVID patients with inflammatory complications and three healthy controls per cell type. Differentially methylated cytosines were identified and analysed by pathway over-representation. Selected pathway-related proteins were measured in plasma from 60 CVID patients and 30 controls and evaluated in three public CVID transcriptomic datasets.ResultsIn this small discovery cohort, CVID was associated with widespread, cell type-specific methylation differences in T-cells and monocytes. T-cells showed a predominance of hypomethylated cytosines and regions, whereas monocytes displayed a more mixed pattern with roughly balanced hypo- and hypermethylation at individual sites. In T-cells, pathway analysis identified Wnt signalling, T-cell differentiation and actin organisation among the top differentially methylated processes. As Wnt signalling is underexplored in CVID and key Wnt modulators are measurable in plasma, we measured Wnt-related proteins in a larger CVID cohort and controls. In plasma, the Wnt antagonists DKK1 and DKK3 were reduced and Wnt agonist RSPO3 increased in CVID. Analyses of three public CVID transcriptomic datasets showed differential expression of Wnt-related genes. Monocyte pathway signals, mainly related to cell adhesion and actin organisation, were more heterogeneous and should be regarded as exploratory given the very small discovery cohort and the inclusion of a patient with a TNFAIP3 variant.ConclusionIn this explorative study we found that CVID is associated with extensive, cell type-specific epigenetic remodelling, particularly in T cells. Wnt signalling emerges as a recurrently altered pathway across DNA methylation, circulating proteins and gene expression, supporting Wnt-related mechanisms as a potential contributor to CVID immunopathology that should be further explored.

14	## Introduction
15	
16	Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is the most common symptomatic primary immunodeficiency in adults, with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 25, 000-50, 000 (1, 2). CVID is characterized by impaired B-cell function leading to decreased immunoglobulin (Ig) production with reduced levels of IgG and IgA, leading to recurrent airway infections with capsulated bacteria (3, 4). Up to 70% of patients also have inflammatory and autoimmune complications, associated with increased morbidity and mortality. These complications appear to be related to dysregulated T-cell and monocyte/macrophage responses (2, 5, 6). Patients with CVID and autoimmune or inflammatory manifestations frequently display a skewed T-cell profile, characterized by enhanced activity of pro-inflammatory T helper cell type 1 cells (Th1), and a reduced number of regulatory T-cells (Treg) (7–9). Moreover, several studies suggest that monocytes/macrophages contribute to these complications through increased production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (10–12). Thus, although B-cell pathology is the hallmark of CVID, persistent activation and functional abnormalities of T-cells and monocytes/macrophages represent critical drivers of the inflammatory and autoimmune phenotype in CVID and may aggravate both immune dysregulation and organ pathology (11, 13).
17	
18	We have recently suggested a role of epigenetic DNA methylation in the aetiology of duodenal inflammation of CVID patients (14). In addition, epigenetic modifications have been proposed as a potential mechanism underlying altered B-cell responses in CVID (15–18). In general, however, data on epigenetic changes in CVID remain limited. To the best of our knowledge, studies specifically addressing epigenetic modifications in relation to T-cell and monocyte pathology are lacking.
19	
20	CpG methylation is a key epigenetic modification where cytosine is converted to 5-methylcytosine (5mC) in DNA. This conversion occurs at 5’-cytosine-phosphate-guanine-3’ (CpG) dinucleotides, and the resulting methylation patterns can be inherited through cell divisions, thereby marking specific cell lineages, but can also change dynamically in response to stimuli such as infections, inflammation, and environmental exposures (19, 20). CpG methylation can interfere with transcription factor binding and other regulatory interactions with DNA, and is therefore an important regulator of gene expression, cell differentiation and immune cell function, acting beyond the inherited DNA (21–23).
21	
22	Given the proposed role of T-cells and monocytes in the pathogenesis of autoimmune and inflammatory complications in CVID, we examined the CpG methylation profile in CD3^+ T-cells and CD14^+ monocytes from this subgroup of CVID patients. Proteins related to the pathways that were most affected by epigenetic regulation were subsequently measured in plasma from a larger CVID cohort. In addition, we explored the relevance of these pathways at transcriptional level by analysing RNA expression data from three independent publicly available CVID cohorts.

25	
26	### Study design
27	
28	In total, six CVID patients were included in the epigenetic analyses (three contributing CD3^+ T-cells and another three contributing CD14^+ monocytes, with no overlap between the patient groups), all enrolled from the Outpatient Clinic at Oslo University Hospital between 2003 and 2005. At inclusion, none had acute infection or exacerbation of a chronic infection, and none received prophylactic antibiotics or immunosuppressive therapy, apart from Ig replacement. CVID was diagnosed according to the 1999 WHO criteria (24), which were the prevailing diagnostic criteria at inclusion. In a retrospective review in 2025, all surviving patients fulfilled the 2019 ESID criteria (25). Age-matched healthy controls (n=6) based on medical history and absence of regular medication were recruited from the same period. All six CVID patients in the WGBS discovery cohort belonged to the non-infectious complication (“complicated CVID”) subgroup and there is no overlap between these patients (Table 1) and those in the plasma cohort (Table 2). Patients were retrospectively screened for monogenic variants using a targeted panel of 598 genes associated with primary immunodeficiency and haematological diseases (https://www.genetikkportalen.no/find-ngs/1100, version 4), which was applied years after recruitment of the discovery cohort.

66	The plasma cohort was recruited at the same department between 2021 and 2024 and included 60 CVID patients fulfilling the 2019 ESID criteria (25) and 30 age-matched healthy controls. As in the epigenetic study, individuals with acute infection, exacerbation of inflammatory/autoimmune disease, or ongoing immunomodulatory therapy (other than Ig replacement) at enrolment were excluded. 68	### Cell isolation
69	
70	Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) were isolated from sodium-heparin anticoagulated blood by density-gradient centrifugation using Lymphoprep (Axis-Shield, Oslo, Norway) within one hour of sampling. CD14^+ monocytes were obtained by positive selection with anti-CD14 Dynabeads, and CD3^+ T-cells by negative selection (T-cell negative isolation kit; both from Dynal, Oslo, Norway). Briefly, PBMCs suspended in PBS with 0.3% BSA were mixed with monodisperse immunomagnetic beads against CD14 (for positive selection of CD14^+ monocytes) and CD14/CD19/CD56 (for negative selection of CD3^+ T-cells) in a cell-to-bead ratio of 1:5. Rosetting cells were isolated magnetically after 30 minutes for either storage (positive selection of monocytes) or disposal (negative selection of T-cells) and the non rosetting fraction (enriched for CD3^+ T cells) was collected. Purity was verified by flow cytometry (27–29). The monocyte fraction contained >95% CD14^+ cells, and the T-cell fraction >90% CD3^+ cells (27). The isolated cells were immediately cryopreserved in liquid nitrogen and remained continuously frozen without repeated freeze-thaw cycles until DNA extraction for WGBS. CVID and control samples were collected, processed and stored identically. DNA quantity and integrity were systematically assessed after thawing, with all WGBS samples showing excellent DNA integrity (DIN 9.0-9.8) (30), indicating minimal degradation despite long-term storage.
71	
72	### Whole-genome bisulphite sequencing
73	
74	DNA was isolated from frozen cell pellets using the Allprep DNA/RNA/Protein kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s instructions with minor modifications. WGBS was performed by Admera Health (NJ, USA), including bisulphite conversion (EZ DNA Methylation-Gold Kit), Accel-NGS Methyl-Seq library preparation and Illumina HiSeq sequencing (150 bp paired-end, approximately 300 million read pairs per sample). Raw reads were quality-filtered and aligned to the hg38 reference genome, and genome-wide 5mC counts were extracted using standard pipelines; full laboratory and bioinformatic details are provided in Supplementary Information.
75	
76	### Plasma analysis of Wnt-related proteins
77	
78	Blood was collected in chilled EDTA tubes, centrifuged within 15 minutes at 2000g for 20 minutes to obtain platelet-poor plasma, aliquoted and stored at -80 °C until a single freeze-thaw. Plasma levels of Dickkopf-1 (DKK1), DKK3, secreted frizzled-related protein 3 (sFRP3), Wnt inhibitory factor (WIF) and R-spondin-3 (RSPO3) were measured by enzyme immunoassays (R&D Systems, Minneapolis, MN, USA). Assays were run in 384-well format using a SELMA pipetting robot and a BioTek dispenser/washer, and absorption was read at 450 nm with 540 nm reference. Intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation were <10% for all measurements.
79	
80	### Wnt expression in previous CVID studies
81	
82	Publicly available mRNA expression data from three studies on CVID and T-cells or PBMC (15, 31, 32) were downloaded and analysed (Supplementary Information). Analyses were restricted to 355 genes annotated to the Gene Ontology “Wnt signalling pathway” (GO:0016055) (33).

84	### Statistical analyses
85	
86	Bioinformatic processing of WGBS and transcriptomic data is outlined in Supplementary Figure S1 and Supplementary Information. Differentially methylated CpG cytosines (DMCs), regions (DMRs) and promoters (DMPs) were identified using R (v4.4.3) with RStudio (v2023.06.0 + 421) and the methylKit (v1.34.0) package, and using Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value <0.05 and a minimum absolute methylation difference of 10%. High- frequency DMCs was defined as subset of DMCs with additional thresholds; at least two DMCs at TSS +- 10kb, could be annotated to a gene, and with a mean methylation difference of at least |25%|. Over-representation analyses (ORA) were performed with Gene Ontology and BH corrected p-values. For each cell type, all significant DMCs, DMRs and DMPs were annotated to genes, and the union of these gene annotations was used as the input gene list for ORA. The background gene set consisted of all genes with at least one CpG site, region or promoter that passed quality filters and was tested for differential methylation in the WGBS data (see Supplementary Information for additional analytical details).
87	
88	Group differences in plasma Wnt-related proteins were assessed in the total cohort (CVID_all vs. healthy controls) and in subgroup analyses (CVID_IO vs. healthy controls, CVID_NIC vs. healthy controls). For each analyte and comparison, distributions were evaluated using the Shapiro-Wilk test. If values were approximately normally distributed (i.e. Shapiro-Wilk > 0.05), an unpaired two-sample t test was applied (this was the case only for DKK1). For skewed analytes, data were log10-transformed and retested for normality; if the log-transformed values were approximately normal, group differences were analysed using t tests on the transformed data, whereas persistently non-normal distributions were compared using Mann-Whitney U tests. Analytes with skewed distributions are plotted on a log10 scale, whereas approximately normally distributed analytes are shown on a linear scale.

90	## Results
91	
92	### Clinical characteristics
93	
94	The epigenetic (CpG) analyses were performed on CD3^+ T-cells and CD14^+ monocytes from three CVID patients with autoimmune/inflammatory complications and three healthy controls in each cell population, corresponding to six different patients and six matched controls in total (Table 1). In the CD14^+ cohort, one CVID patient was later found to carry a monogenic TNFAIP3 variant, while the CD3^+ T-cell cohort included three CVID patients without identified monogenic variants. This TNFAIP3 variant was first described in a CVID patient in 2020 (34) and was therefore not included in the original gene panels. No other CVID patients in this cohort had pathogenic variants detected by the gene panel.
95	
96	### CpG methylation patterns separate CVID from healthy controls
97	
98	CpG site coverages showed the highest frequency at about five reads per CpG site, with a genome-wide CpG coverage range from 12 to 35 million sites per sample, after read filtering (Supplementary Figure S2, S3, S4A). More than 1.6 million CpG sites were included in the analysis for both cell types, in addition to over 750, 000 CpG regions and over 72, 000 promoters (Supplementary Figure S4B). These data were then used to compare CpG methylation patterns between CVID patients and healthy controls.
99	
100	We first performed hierarchical clustering using all retained CpG regions in CD3^+ T cells and CD14^+ monocytes, which provided a global overview but showed limited visual separation between CVID and healthy controls (Supplementary Figure S5A-B). In contrast, hierarchical clustering based on all identified DMRs in each cell type yielded a clear separation of the groups consistent with the use of regions showing statistically significant methylation differences (Supplementary Figure S5C-D). Partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), applied as a supervised approach to maximize separation between groups, also showed a similar separation between CVID patients and healthy controls in both cell types (Figures 1A, B).

104	### Differentially methylated CpG sites, regions and promoters in CD3^+ T-cells in CVID
105	
106	To pinpoint where these epigenetic differences occur in the genome, differential CpG methylation was next assessed at three levels: (i) individual CpG cytosines showing significant methylation differences between groups (DMCs), (ii) genomic regions containing clustered CpGs that were consistently hyper- or hypomethylated (DMRs), and (iii) promoter-associated CpG sites identified as differentially methylated (DMPs).
107	
108	In T-cells, comparison of CVID patients to healthy controls revealed 486 DMCs and 3, 723 DMRs (Figure 2A). Approximately two thirds of these DMCs and DMRs were hypomethylated in CVID, which may reflect enhanced activation, whereas the remaining one-third were hypermethylated, which may reflect suppressed activation (35). For promoter-associated probes, 420 DMPs were detected in CVID CD3^+ cells compared to controls. In contrast to DMCs/DMRs, roughly two-thirds of the DMPs were hypermethylated and one-third hypomethylated (Figure 2A). This contrasting pattern between DMCs/DMRs and DMPs was statistically supported by chi-square tests comparing the proportions of hyper- and hypomethylated sites across these categories (Supplementary Figure S6). The majority of DMCs and DMRs localized to intergenic or intronic DNA regions, whereas promoter and exon location were underrepresented (Figure 2B). Because DMPs are by definition promoter-associated, this difference in genomic distribution may partly account for the divergent hyper-to hypomethylation balance observed between DMCs/DMRs and DMPs.

112	### Differentially methylated CpG sites, regions and promoters in CD14^+ monocytes in CVID
113	
114	In CD14^+ monocytes, comparison of CVID patients to controls identified 341 DMCs, 3, 057 DMRs, and 268 DMPs (Figure 2A). 116	### Overall methylation patterns and summary of tested regions
117	
118	Collectively, the CpG analyses in this small discovery cohort indicate numerous methylation differences between CVID and healthy controls. While T-cells were characterized mainly by hypomethylated DMCs and DMRs, monocytes showed a more even distribution of hypo- and hypermethylation across these categories. Chi-square tests nevertheless demonstrated statistically significant differences in hyper- versus hypomethylation between DMCs/DMRs and DMPs in both cell types, with substantially stronger effects in CD3^+ T-cells (Supplementary Figure S6). In both cell types, most epigenetic alterations were captured by DMRs (contiguous genomic regions with coordinated methylation changes) that may function as regulators of gene expression, cell differentiation, and disease processes (21–23, 36). All DMCs, DMRs, and DMPs are provided in Supplementary Excel File S1. Volcano plots showing methylation difference versus statistical significance for all tested regions in CD3^+ T-cells and CD14^+ monocytes are included in Supplementary Figure S7. The plots include approximately 800, 000 regions and are therefore heavily overplotted but are included as an overall summary of the methylation landscape.

120	### Wnt signalling among the top differentially methylated pathways in CD3^+ T-cells
121	
122	We next performed over-representation analysis (ORA) using the Gene Ontology database to identify enriched biological pathways related to CpG methylation. Actin, beyond its role in cell motility, reorganizes in T-cells following T-cell receptor activation (37). Wnt signalling encompasses several pathways that regulate cell shape, motility, and differentiation, and play a critical role in T-cell development and function, including interacting with signalling molecules such as JNK and mTOR (36, 38–40). The overlap between selected pathways is shown in Figure 3B.

156	## Discussion
157	
158	To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to explore genome-wide CpG methylation in purified T-cells and monocytes in CVID. We report two main novel observations: first, that CD3^+ T-cells and CD14^+ monocytes show evidence of cell type-specific epigenetic alterations; and second, that Wnt signalling emerges as a recurrently altered pathway, supported across DNA methylation data, circulating Wnt-related proteins and independent transcriptomic datasets. Taken together, these findings point to previously unrecognized epigenetic and Wnt-related mechanisms that may contribute to the immunological phenotype of CVID.
159	
160	Previous epigenetic work in CVID is limited and has mainly focused on B-cells and duodenal tissue (14–18). In parallel, large genetic studies have identified monogenic causes in only a subset of patients, leaving the majority without a clear genetic explanation (11). This has raised the possibility that epigenetic mechanisms in other immune cell types, such as T-cells and monocytes, may contribute to disease pathogenesis. Although our discovery cohort is small, whole-genome bisulphite sequencing atlases in other tissues indicate that methylation profiles within a given cell type are highly reproducible across individuals when at least three samples are analysed (46). Our data add an important layer by showing CpG methylation differences in CD3^+ T-cells and CD14^+ monocytes from CVID patients with inflammatory complications. The predominance of hypomethylated DMCs/DMRs in T-cells is compatible with an “open” chromatin landscape and activated or poised states, which fits well with reports of skewed Th1 responses, reduced Treg frequencies and chronic T-cell activation in CVID (7–9). In monocytes, a more balanced pattern of hypo- and hypermethylation may reflect that epigenetic modifications in these cells contribute to the coexistence of pro- and anti-inflammatory programmes, consistent with increased cytokine production and altered innate responses described in this disease (10–12).
161	
162	A novel finding of this study is the involvement of Wnt signalling across several molecular levels. Wnt is increasingly recognized as a key regulator of T-cell differentiation, memory formation and tolerance, as well as of haematopoietic stem cell and progenitor function (38). In experimental models, canonical and non-canonical Wnt pathways influence T-cell survival, the balance between effector and regulatory subsets, and the propensity for exhaustion, partly through crosstalk with mTOR and NF-κB (38, 39, 47–49). In this context, the prominent Wnt signal in our epigenetic data is notable. Importantly, Wnt pathway alterations have also been reported in duodenal tissue from CVID enteropathy, where RNA sequencing has shown downregulation of Wnt signalling in villous atrophy lesions, suggesting epithelial involvement (50). Pathway analyses identified Wnt among the top differentially methylated pathways in CD3^+ T-cells, alongside immune pathways such as T-cell differentiation and actin organisation. Clustering of Wnt related DMRs clearly separated CVID from controls and showed coherent patterns across patients, suggesting a shared disease associated imprint rather than random noise. That this signature emerged in purified T-cells, and in the absence of known monogenic variants in the T-cell cohort, is compatible with the notion that Wnt-related methylation changes could be a genuine feature of CVID T-cell biology. The Wnt signal in the epigenetic analyses was further supported at the transcriptomic and protein levels.
163	
164	When measuring selected Wnt proteins in plasma from CVID patients and healthy controls, we found that CVID patients had reduced plasma levels of DKK1 and DKK3, inhibitors of the canonical Wnt/β-catenin signalling pathway, and increased levels of RSPO3, an activator of this pathway, potentially suggesting a net enhancement of canonical Wnt activation in CVID. Subgroup analyses showed no significant differences between “CVID complicated” and “CVID infection only”, but these analyses were weakened by the low number of patients in the “CVID infection only” group, consistent with limited statistical power. One could speculate that these patterns may suggest that the disturbed Wnt profile is related to the immunodeficiency per se, but the available data do not allow any firm conclusion. An alternative interpretation is that these Wnt-related changes primarily reflect chronic immune dysregulation and inflammatory complications rather than CVID (i.e. B-cell deficiency) per se, and larger, well-characterised cohorts will be required to disentangle pathway signatures related to complicated CVID from those related to CVID more broadly.
165	
166	While plasma measurements cannot pinpoint cellular sources, this pattern is consistent with an overall shift towards enhanced Wnt activity in CVID. Reanalysis of three independent CVID transcriptomic datasets, showing recurrent differential expression of Wnt-related genes with overlap to our methylation findings, provides an additional, external line of support. Overall, these observations suggest that Wnt signalling is not an incidental finding confined to a single dataset, but a recurrent pathway in CVID.
167	
168	From a mechanistic standpoint, altered Wnt activity might contribute not only to autoimmune and inflammatory complications, but also to more fundamental features of CVID, such as impaired regulatory T-cell function (47). Moreover, β-catenin, as an important mediator in canonical Wnt signalling, has been reported to be dispensable for normal B-cell development and function, and is therefore unlikely to underlie the B-cell maturation defect seen in CVID (51). Functional studies will be required to test these hypotheses, and to determine whether Wnt related changes have direct causal roles in CVID pathogenesis. Of interest, the Wnt signalling pathway has emerged as a novel target for therapy in various disorders (38), including approaches targeting RSPO3, which was upregulated in the present CVID plasma cohort (52).
169	
170	Wnt has not previously been systematically explored in CVID, and several key Wnt modulators are measurable in plasma, which made this pathway particularly suitable for further, hypothesis-driven investigation. This does not imply that Wnt is more important than other enriched pathways such as actin organisation or T-cell differentiation. Our plasma protein analyses and the Wnt-focused re-analysis of public RNA datasets should therefore be viewed as targeted follow-up of one underexplored pathway, and we acknowledge that this post hoc focus introduces a risk of confirmation bias compared with an unbiased pathway screen. Overall, our findings highlight Wnt signalling as a recurrent and mechanistically attractive axis alongside other pathways in CVID, without establishing it as the only or uniquely dominant pathway.
171	
172	In CD14^+ monocytes, exploratory pathway analysis highlighted processes related to cell adhesion, actin organisation and synaptic/neurological signalling. These pathways are relevant for monocyte trafficking, phagocytosis and immune synapse formation, and are in line with reports suggesting that monocytes/macrophages contribute to tissue inflammation and autoimmunity in CVID (10–12). Interpretation of the monocyte data is, however, complicated by the presence of a TNFAIP3 (A20) variant in one of the three CVID patients. Our separate pathway analyses of this individual’s monocytes indicated hypomethylation in pathways related to Fc gamma receptor-mediated phagocytosis and patterns compatible with altered NF-κB-related regulation, in line with the known biology of TNFAIP3 (34) and supporting the validity of our analytical approach. As the heatmaps suggest, this patient does not appear as a clear outlier for the main CD14^+ pathway findings, illustrating how patients with a defined monogenic variant and those without an identified genetic cause can converge on similar pathway level and epigenetic changes. This resonates with the ongoing discussion about whether patients with identified monogenic defects should still be classified under CVID or considered as separate entities (11, 53).
173	
174	Important limitations must be acknowledged. First, the discovery cohort is very small, which makes WGBS-based identification of differentially methylated CpGs and regions susceptible to inter-individual variability, batch effects and reduced statistical power. The discovery cohort did not include cells from CVID patients with “infection only”, and the monocyte data are further complicated by the presence of a TNFAIP3 variant in one of the three CVID patients, whereas the CD3^+ T-cell cohort comprised CVID patients without identified monogenic defects. Although our clustering and variant-specific pathway analyses indicate that the main actin/adhesion-related signals are not solely driven by this carrier, the very small sample size precludes robust sensitivity analyses excluding this patient, and the monocyte results should therefore be interpreted with particular caution. Furthermore, the epigenetic analyses were performed on bulk CD3^+ T-cells and CD14^+ monocytes and did not include cellular subsets. An additional limitation is the substantial time gap between the discovery and validation cohorts. Cohort composition, genetic work-up and unmeasured secular changes in CVID care may therefore differ over time. However, the core principles of immunoglobulin replacement therapy have remained comparable across this period, and patients receiving immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory drugs were excluded from both cohorts, so major changes in such therapies are unlikely to have directly influenced our results. The cross-sectional design, the lack of functional assays of Wnt pathway activation in CVID cells (e.g. reporter assays or downstream target gene readouts), the lack of adjustment for kidney function and bone metabolism, both of which could influence levels of Wnt modulators (54), the absence of histone modification data, which are important mediators of epigenetic regulation, further limits our ability to infer causality from the observed methylation and plasma protein patterns. Taken together, these limitations mean that the epigenetic results should be regarded as exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than definitive.
175	
176	## Conclusions
177	
178	In conclusion, this exploratory study provides initial evidence that CVID is associated with cell type-specific epigenetic remodelling in T-cells and monocytes, and identifies Wnt signalling as a recurrently altered pathway across DNA methylation, circulating proteins, and independent transcriptomic datasets. In the context of existing literature, these findings support an emerging concept of CVID as a disorder of broader immune reprogramming beyond B-cell dysfunction and highlight Wnt signalling and related regulatory networks as promising targets for future mechanistic and, potentially, therapeutic exploration. However, these issues need to be more thoroughly studied in larger cohorts with prospective follow-up and mechanistic experiments.

messages.content: 94	The epigenetic (CpG) analyses were performed on CD3^+ T-cells and CD14^+ monocytes from three CVID patients with autoimmune/inflammatory complications and three healthy controls in each cell population, corresponding to six different patients and six matched controls in total (Table 1). In the CD14^+ cohort, one CVID patient was later found to carry a monogenic TNFAIP3 variant, while the CD3^+ T-cell cohort included three CVID patients without identified monogenic variants. This TNFAIP3 variant was first described in a CVID patient in 2020 (34) and was therefore not included in the original gene panels. No other CVID patients in this cohort had pathogenic variants detected by the gene panel.

134	Since CVID is a heterogeneous condition and one of the three CD14^+ CVID patients carried a TNFAIP3 (A20) variant, we performed a separate pathway analysis of this individual’s monocytes. This analysis revealed hypomethylation in pathways related to Fc gamma receptor-mediated phagocytosis, together with patterns consistent with altered inflammatory/NF-κB related regulation, in line with the known role of TNFAIP3/A20 (11, 34) (Supplementary Excel File S4). Because patients with monogenic and non-monogenic CVID can share similar clinical phenotypes (43, 44), we next examined whether this individual disproportionately influenced the pathway level results. As shown in Figure 4C and Supplementary Figures S8B-C, the TNFAIP3 carrier clustered together with the other CVID patients across all overlapping methylation regions in shared pathways, suggesting that the main CD14^+ pathway signals are not driven solely by this variant. All ORA results are provided in Supplementary Excel File S2-4. Our main conclusions are based on pathway-level findings, and we have taken care to assess their robustness by variant-specific analyses and by demonstrating that the TNFAIP3 carrier clusters with the other CVID patients across the key enriched pathways. The inclusion of this patient is still a limitation of our monocyte data.

28	In total, six CVID patients were included in the epigenetic analyses (three contributing CD3^+ T-cells and another three contributing CD14^+ monocytes, with no overlap between the patient groups), all enrolled from the Outpatient Clinic at Oslo University Hospital between 2003 and 2005. At inclusion, none had acute infection or exacerbation of a chronic infection, and none received prophylactic antibiotics or immunosuppressive therapy, apart from Ig replacement. CVID was diagnosed according to the 1999 WHO criteria (24), which were the prevailing diagnostic criteria at inclusion. In a retrospective review in 2025, all surviving patients fulfilled the 2019 ESID criteria (25). Age-matched healthy controls (n=6) based on medical history and absence of regular medication were recruited from the same period. All six CVID patients in the WGBS discovery cohort belonged to the non-infectious complication (“complicated CVID”) subgroup and there is no overlap between these patients (Table 1) and those in the plasma cohort (Table 2). Patients were retrospectively screened for monogenic variants using a targeted panel of 598 genes associated with primary immunodeficiency and haematological diseases (https://www.genetikkportalen.no/find-ngs/1100, version 4), which was applied years after recruitment of the discovery cohort.

138	Given that the Wnt-related methylation signal in CD3^+ T-cells were among the most prominent signals, and in light of the recognised importance of this pathway in T-cell function and autoimmunity (38, 41), we next examined whether Wnt pathway involvement was also reflected at the systemic protein level. We address this we measured five secreted Wnt modulators in plasma from a larger cohort comprising 60 CVID patients (37 women, 62%; mean age 43 years) and 30 healthy controls (18 women, 60%; mean age 45 years) (Table 2). The Wnt modulators included four extracellular antagonists (DKK1, DKK3, sFRP3 and WIF), and one extracellular agonist (RSPO3).
